rationale: A wins because it stays closer to the facts and turns the missing reliability number into the sharpest story: "Replit's new agent builds and ships working apps for people who can't code — and won't say how often they break." B has the same good instinct, but it keeps freelancing in the headlines: "ships a whole working app from one English sentence" and "You pay per build" both add specificity the update does not provide. That is not color; that is how you hand a reporter an avoidable correction.
gaps_in_A: "ahead of course planning for the coming academic year" is a plausible seasonal peg, but it is not in the supplied update. Use it only if someone verifies the academic-calendar timing.
"When the software writes itself, you pay by the job" implies a pricing unit the update does not give. The supplied fact is usage-based pricing on top of subscriptions, not per job.

"The story is a non-engineer who described an app in plain English and is running it in production" is a good customer-story frame, but it is not currently pitchable without the named user the update lacks.
gaps_in_B: "from one English sentence" invents specificity. The update says plain-English description, not one sentence.
"Replit is betting class on it" overstates the education angle. The update says Replit is used heavily in education; it does not say the agent is being pushed into classrooms.
"which is most students before a course, not after" is an inference stacked on an inference. Fine as a question, too dressed up as a premise.
"You pay per build" is unsupported. The update says usage-based pricing, but not that the metered unit is a build.
